rules.title: PowerShell with an encoded command
rules.description: PowerShell started with -EncodedCommand (or any short form PowerShell accepts, such as -enc, -en, -ec or -e) followed by a Base64 blob. Attackers use it to hide the real script from command-line logging and simple string matching. Admin tools rarely need it.
triage: Decode the Base64 (it is UTF-16LE) and read the actual script.
Check the parent process. Office, a browser or a script host as parent is a strong signal.
Look for network connections and child processes from the same PowerShell process in the next minutes.
If the decoded script downloads or runs code, isolate the host and collect the payload.
false_positives: Configuration management agents (SCCM, some RMM tools) that wrap scripts in -EncodedCommand.
Vendor installers that pass a short encoded bootstrap.
rules.xql:
config case_sensitive = false
| dataset = xdr_data
| filter event_type = ENUM.PROCESS and event_sub_type = ENUM.PROCESS_START
| filter (action_process_image_name in ("powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe") and action_process_image_command_line ~= "(?i)\\s[-/]e(c|n\\w*)?\\s+[A-Za-z0-9+/]{16,}={0,2}") and not ((actor_process_image_name != null and actor_process_image_name = "ccmexec.exe"))
| fields _time, agent_hostname, actor_effective_username, actor_process_image_name, action_process_image_name, action_process_image_command_line
| sort desc _time
| limit 1000
rules.spl:
`sysmon` EventCode=1
| eval process_name=lower(mvindex(split(Image,"\\"),-1)), parent_name=lower(mvindex(split(ParentImage,"\\"),-1))
| where ((lower(process_name)="powershell.exe" OR lower(process_name)="pwsh.exe") AND match(CommandLine, "(?i)\\s[-/]e(c|n\\w*)?\\s+[A-Za-z0-9+/]{16,}={0,2}")) AND NOT ((isnotnull(parent_name) AND lower(parent_name)="ccmexec.exe"))
| table _time host User ParentImage Image CommandLine
| sort - _time

rules.title: PowerShell download cradle that runs what it fetched
rules.description: PowerShell downloads content (Net.WebClient, Invoke-WebRequest, Invoke-RestMethod, BITS) and runs it in memory with Invoke-Expression. This is the classic first-stage loader. Downloading alone is common for admins, so the rule needs both halves.
triage: Pull the URL out of the command line and check its reputation and when the domain was registered.
Fetch the payload from an isolated sandbox, not from the endpoint.
Check for files written and connections made right after the event.
false_positives: Installers for developer tools that pipe a script from the vendor (for example some package manager bootstraps).

rules.title: Office application starts a shell or script host
rules.description: Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook or another Office app starts cmd, PowerShell, a script host or a LOLBin. This is what a malicious macro or an exploited document looks like on the endpoint. Office almost never needs to do this on its own.
triage: Identify the document the Office process had open and where it came from (mail attachment, download, share).
Read the child command line and follow any download or new process it started.
Search for the same document hash or sender across other mailboxes and endpoints.
false_positives: Business macros that call cmd or PowerShell on purpose. Build an allowlist by document path and signer.

rules.title: mshta runs a remote HTA or inline script
rules.description: mshta.exe executes an HTA from a URL or inline JavaScript/VBScript. It is a signed Microsoft binary, so it is a favourite way to run script while bypassing application allowlisting.
triage: Retrieve the URL or inline script from the command line and analyse it in a sandbox.
Check child processes and network connections of mshta.
false_positives: Very old line-of-business apps built on HTA that load pages from an intranet server.

rules.title: regsvr32 loads a remote scriptlet (Squiblydoo)
rules.description: regsvr32 with /i:<URL> and scrobj.dll fetches and runs a COM scriptlet from the internet. The technique is called Squiblydoo. Legitimate COM registration never points at a URL.
triage: Pull the scriptlet URL and analyse the .sct content.
Check for child processes of regsvr32 and outbound connections.
false_positives: None expected. Investigate every hit.

rules.title: rundll32 runs script or loads from a URL
rules.description: rundll32 is used to run JavaScript through mshtml (RunHTMLApplication) or to load content from a URL or WebDAV path. Normal rundll32 use names a local DLL and an export.
triage: Identify the DLL or script being loaded and get a copy from the path or URL.
Check the parent process to see how rundll32 was launched.
false_positives: Rare. Some printer or update utilities pass a URL as an argument to their own DLL. Allowlist by DLL path.

rules.title: Script host runs a script from a user-writable folder
rules.description: wscript or cscript runs a .js, .jse, .vbs, .vbe or .wsf file from AppData, Temp, Downloads or Public. This is how many phishing ZIP attachments start their chain.
triage: Get the script file and read it (deobfuscate JScript if needed).
Find how it arrived, usually an email attachment or a browser download in the minutes before.
false_positives: Logon scripts or helpdesk scripts copied to a user profile. Allowlist by script hash.

rules.description: wmic process call create starts a program through WMI. With /node it runs on a remote machine, which is a common lateral movement method. Admins mostly use other tools today.
triage: Note any /node target and check that host for the started process.
Confirm the account and whether it normally administers that host.
false_positives: Older admin scripts and some software deployment tools.

rules.title: Run key points to a user-writable path or a script host
rules.description: A value is written under ...\CurrentVersion\Run or RunOnce and its data points into AppData, Temp, Public or ProgramData, or launches a script host or LOLBin. This is the most common way commodity malware survives a reboot.
triage: Check the binary or script the value points to (signature, hash, age, prevalence across the fleet).
Identify the process that wrote the value and its own origin.
Remove the value only after collecting the payload.
false_positives: Per-user installs (Teams, Zoom, OneDrive, Discord, Spotify) live in AppData. Allowlist by signer and exact path.

Check the account the task runs as and who created it.
false_positives: Software updaters that register their own task from AppData (browsers, chat apps).

If the command targeted another host (sc \\host create), investigate that host too.
false_positives: Installers that create a service from ProgramData. Allowlist by signer.

Treat the host as compromised until proven otherwise; look at the 30 minutes before for the access path.
Check whether the same command ran on other hosts (it often runs fleet-wide before encryption).
false_positives: Exclusions pushed by IT for backup or database software. These should come from GPO or Intune, not an interactive shell.

rules.title: Windows event logs cleared from the command line
rules.description: wevtutil cl, Clear-EventLog, Remove-EventLog or the .NET ClearLog call wipe event logs to destroy evidence. Admins very rarely clear logs by hand.
triage: Look for event 1102 (Security log cleared) and 104 (System log cleared) from the same time.
Pull logs from the SIEM or EDR for the period before the wipe, they are still there.
false_positives: Lab or golden-image build scripts that reset logs before sealing an image.

rules.title: Script host or LOLBin looks up a paste site, file drop or tunnel service
rules.description: PowerShell, a script host or a LOLBin resolves pastebin, raw GitHub content, a temporary file host, an ngrok or Cloudflare tunnel, Discord CDN or the Telegram bot API. These free services host payloads and act as C2 because they are rarely blocked.
triage: Find the URL in proxy logs or the process command line and fetch the content safely.
Check what the process did after the lookup (new files, child processes).
false_positives: Admin or developer scripts that pull from raw.githubusercontent.com. Allowlist by script and repo.

| dataset = xdr_data
| filter event_type = ENUM.NETWORK and dns_query_name != null
| filter actor_process_image_name in ("powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "wscript.exe", "cscript.exe", "mshta.exe", "rundll32.exe", "regsvr32.exe", "certutil.exe", "bitsadmin.exe", "cmd.exe", "msbuild.exe") and dns_query_name ~= "(?i)(^|\\.)(pastebin\\.com|paste\\.ee|hastebin\\.com|rentry\\.co|raw\\.githubusercontent\\.com|transfer\\.sh|file\\.io|gofile\\.io|temp\\.sh|ngrok\\.io|ngrok-free\\.app|trycloudflare\\.com|cdn\\.discordapp\\.com|api\\.telegram\\.org)\\.?$"
| fields _time, agent_hostname, actor_process_image_name, dns_query_name
| sort desc _time
| limit 1000

`sysmon` EventCode=22
| eval process_name=lower(mvindex(split(Image,"\\"),-1))

rules.title: rclone copies data to a remote
rules.description: rclone (often renamed) syncing or copying folders to cloud storage, MEGA, FTP or WebDAV. It is the most used exfiltration tool in ransomware intrusions because it is fast and looks like backup traffic.
triage: Read the remote name and find the rclone.conf to learn the destination and credentials.
Measure how much data left (proxy or firewall bytes out) and which folders were copied.
false_positives: IT backup jobs that use rclone on purpose. These should run from a fixed path and account.

config case_sensitive = false
| dataset = xdr_data
| filter event_type = ENUM.PROCESS and event_sub_type = ENUM.PROCESS_START
| filter action_process_image_command_line ~= "(?i)\\s(copy|copyto|sync|move)\\s" and (action_process_image_name = "rclone.exe" or (action_process_image_command_line contains "--multi-thread-streams" or action_process_image_command_line contains "--no-check-certificate" or action_process_image_command_line contains "--transfers" or action_process_image_command_line contains "--ignore-existing" or action_process_image_command_line contains "--max-age" or action_process_image_command_line contains "--auto-confirm"))
| fields _time, agent_hostname, actor_effective_username, actor_process_image_name, action_process_image_name, action_process_image_command_line
| sort desc _time
| limit 1000
rules.spl:
`sysmon` EventCode=1
| eval process_name=lower(mvindex(split(Image,"\\"),-1)), parent_name=lower(mvindex(split(ParentImage,"\\"),-1))
| where match(CommandLine, "(?i)\\s(copy|copyto|sync|move)\\s") AND (lower(process_name)="rclone.exe" OR (match(CommandLine, "(?i)\\-\\-multi\\-thread\\-streams") OR match(CommandLine, "(?i)\\-\\-no\\-check\\-certificate") OR match(CommandLine, "(?i)\\-\\-transfers") OR match(CommandLine, "(?i)\\-\\-ignore\\-existing") OR match(CommandLine, "(?i)\\-\\-max\\-age") OR match(CommandLine, "(?i)\\-\\-auto\\-confirm")))
| table _time host User ParentImage Image CommandLine
| sort - _time

rules.title: Shadow copies, backups or boot recovery removed
rules.description: vssadmin or WMI deleting shadow copies, shrinking shadow storage, wbadmin deleting the backup catalog, or bcdedit disabling recovery. Ransomware does this minutes before or during encryption so the victim cannot roll back.
rules.condition_text: vssadmin or wmic or powershell or wbadmin or bcdedit
triage: Treat as active ransomware. Isolate the host now, then investigate.
Check other hosts for the same command in the same minutes; it is usually pushed everywhere at once.
false_positives: Backup software rotating its own shadow copies (usually through the VSS API, not vssadmin).

rules.title: PowerView or PowerSploit AD recon functions on the command line
rules.description: PowerView and PowerSploit functions that map users, groups, ACLs, sessions, shares, local admin access and trusts (Get-DomainUser, Find-InterestingDomainAcl, Invoke-ShareFinder, Find-LocalAdminAccess, Get-DomainTrust...). In an AD intrusion this is the step that finds the path to Domain Admin.
triage: Find out how PowerView got there. It is usually loaded in memory, so check PowerShell 4104 script blocks (DL-0044) on the same host.

triage.Look at what came next from the same acc: ACL changes (DL-0034, 5136 events), new logons on servers, Kerberos ticket requests.

false_positives: Authorised penetration tests. Some AD audit scripts reuse PowerView function names.

rules.title: Rubeus requests, forges or injects Kerberos tickets
rules.description: Rubeus verbs used after the first foothold: asktgt with a hash or key (overpass-the-hash), s4u (delegation abuse), ptt (pass-the-ticket), tgtdeleg, golden, silver and diamond ticket forging, and monitor (catching TGTs on a host with unconstrained delegation). Also catches Rubeus run through an in-memory loader, since the arguments stay on the command line.
triage: /rc4: or /aes256: means a stolen key is being used: find where it came from (LSASS dump, DCSync) and reset that account.
s4u with /impersonateuser points to delegation abuse: check msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity and msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo on the target service.
golden, silver or diamond means forged tickets. Plan a double krbtgt reset if krbtgt keys were exposed.
false_positives: Red team exercises. klist and normal Kerberos use do not match.

rules.title: AD CS abuse tool looks for or requests vulnerable certificates
rules.description: Certify, Certipy and ForgeCert used to find vulnerable certificate templates (ESC1 to ESC8), request a certificate as another user, or forge one with a stolen CA key. A certificate gives a login that survives password resets.
triage: Check CA events 4886 and 4887 for certificates issued to the same requester around that time (DL-0061).
Revoke any certificate issued to a privileged account that was not expected, and fix the template (enrollment rights, ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT, Certificate Request Agent EKU).
false_positives: PKI admins auditing templates with Certify or Certipy find. Confirm with the PKI team.

rules.title: In-memory .NET loader runs an offensive tool
rules.description: Loaders such as NetLoader take a path or URL to a .NET assembly, patch AMSI and ETW, and run the tool from memory so it never touches disk (Loader.exe -path ... -args ...). The tool names usually stay visible in the arguments.
triage: The URL in -path is often a local port forward (netsh portproxy, DL-0035) to the attacker's server. Find the listener.
Read the -args value. It tells you which tool ran and what it did (DL-0031 for Rubeus, DL-0019 for SafetyKatz).
false_positives: Rare. Some deployment tools accept -path and -args; they do not point at offensive assemblies.

rules.title: AD object rights or memberships changed with PowerView or StandIn
rules.description: Write actions from PowerView and StandIn: granting rights on an object (Add-DomainObjectAcl, including DCSync rights), setting attributes (Set-DomainObject), adding group members, resetting passwords, or writing resource-based constrained delegation (StandIn --computer --sid). These turn a weak ACL into a working escalation path.
triage: On the DC, find the matching 5136 (attribute changed) or 4728/4732/4756 (member added) events and the object that changed.
Undo the change, then look for what the attacker did with it next (new delegation, DCSync, password reset logon).
false_positives: AD administrators using PowerView in scripts. Uncommon; most admins use the ActiveDirectory module.

rules.title: netsh port proxy set up to forward traffic
rules.description: netsh interface portproxy add v4tov4 makes Windows forward a local port to another host. Attackers use it to reach their tool server from a segmented host, for example to serve an in-memory loader over http://127.0.0.1:8080, or to pivot to an internal service.
triage: Run netsh interface portproxy show all on the host and check where connectaddress points.
Look for downloads from 127.0.0.1 on the listen port right after (loaders, DL-0033).
false_positives: Admins forwarding a port for a legacy application. These are long-lived and documented.

rules.description: net localgroup administrators <user> /add, or Add-LocalGroupMember. Local privilege escalation exploits (for example a service abuse with PowerUp) often end with exactly this command run as SYSTEM.
triage: Check the parent. services.exe or a vulnerable service binary as parent means local privilege escalation through a service.
Remove the account from the group and find how it got SYSTEM.
false_positives: Build scripts and helpdesk tools that grant local admin. They run from known parents and accounts.

rules.title: Service binary path changed with sc config
rules.description: sc config <service> binPath= points an existing service at a new command. With weak service permissions, any user can do this and get code running as SYSTEM on the next service start. PowerUp's Invoke-ServiceAbuse does the same thing.

Restore the service config and fix the service ACL (sc sdshow).
false_positives: Software installers reconfiguring their own service. They do not point binPath at cmd.exe or net.exe.

triage: Read COR_PROFILER_PATH. A DLL in a user folder means a bypass, not an APM agent.

rules.title: DSRM administrator allowed to log on normally (DsrmAdminLogonBehavior)
rules.description: Setting DsrmAdminLogonBehavior to 2 lets the Directory Services Restore Mode administrator, a local account on every DC whose password rarely changes, log on over the network. An attacker who dumped that hash keeps a backdoor into the DC.

triage: Put the value back and reboot. Assume credentials on this host after the change are exposed.

rules.title: AMSI or ETW bypass in a PowerShell script block
rules.description: PowerShell script block logging (event 4104) records the code PowerShell actually ran, after decoding. Bypasses that switch off AMSI (amsiInitFailed, AmsiScanBuffer patching, amsi.dll tricks) or blind ETW (EtwEventWrite, PSEtwLogProvider) leave their strings here, even when the command line is obfuscated.
triage: Read the next script blocks from the same host and session. The bypass is the first step; the tool loaded after it is the real payload (DL-0044).
Check if the user also set COR_PROFILER (DL-0040) to hide later activity.
false_positives: Security tools and training material that mention AMSI. Real bypasses use reflection on these names.

rules.title: Offensive PowerShell toolkit loaded (PowerView, PowerUp, Invoke-Mimikatz)

Look for the AMSI bypass just before it (DL-0043) and the account that ran it.

rules.title: Security descriptor backdoor on WMI, PS Remoting, remote registry or AdminSDHolder
rules.description: Nishang and DAMP functions that quietly give an account remote access by editing security descriptors: Set-RemoteWMI, Set-RemotePSRemoting, Add-RemoteRegBackdoor, plus AdminSDHolder and DCSync rights added with PowerView. These are classic domain persistence techniques because nothing new is created, only permissions change.
triage: On the target host, review the security descriptors of root\cimv2, the PSRemoting session configuration, and the winreg key.
Compare the AdminSDHolder ACL with a known good copy and remove unknown principals.
false_positives: Very rare outside red team work.

rules.title: DCSync, directory replication requested by an account that is not a DC
rules.description: Event 4662 on a domain controller with the replication rights GUIDs (DS-Replication-Get-Changes and -All) means someone asked the DC to replicate secrets, the way mimikatz lsadump::dcsync works. Domain controllers do this all the time; a user account should never do it.
rules.condition_text: access and replication and not dc_account
triage: Treat as domain compromise. Find the source IP from the matching 4624 logon on the DC.
Find out which account was replicated (krbtgt, Administrator, trust accounts). If krbtgt: plan a double reset.
Remove replication rights from any account that should not hold them (Get-DomainObjectAcl on the domain root).
false_positives: Azure AD Connect (MSOL_ accounts) and some backup or identity products replicate on purpose. Exclude them by name.

rules.title: Kerberos service ticket with RC4 for a user service account (Kerberoasting)
rules.description: Event 4769 with ticket encryption 0x17 (RC4) for a service that is not a computer account and not krbtgt. In a domain that uses AES, RC4 service tickets for user accounts with an SPN are what Kerberoasting tools request, because RC4 is the fastest to crack offline.
rules.condition_text: tgs and not machine_or_krbtgt and not krbtgt
triage: Many 4769 RC4 requests from one account in a short time is Kerberoasting. A single one may be an old client.
Give the targeted service accounts long random passwords or move them to gMSA.
false_positives: Old applications and service accounts still limited to RC4. Fix them (msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes) and the rule gets quiet.

false_positives: Accounts that really need no pre-auth (rare, some old Unix integrations). List them and review why.

rules.title: TGT requested with RC4 encryption (possible overpass-the-hash)

Disable RC4 in the domain where possible, so this becomes a high-fidelity signal.
false_positives: Accounts and devices that only support RC4. They are the same every day, so baseline them.

false_positives: Smart card and Windows Hello for Business logons. Exclude the accounts and devices that use them.

false_positives: Web and SQL front ends that use constrained delegation. Baseline which services delegate to which.

rules.description: Event 5136 changing msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo. The account can then get tickets as any user for the listed services, and the service name in the ticket can be swapped for another service on the same host (for example TIME to LDAP or CIFS).

Prefer resource-based delegation scoped to the exact service, and mark admins as not delegatable.

rules.title: Key credential added to an account (shadow credentials)
rules.description: Event 5136 writing msDS-KeyCredentialLink. Windows Hello for Business writes this attribute on enrollment, but an attacker with write rights on an account can add their own key and then log on as that account with a certificate (PKINIT), without knowing or changing its password.

Expect a PKINIT logon for the same account soon after (DL-0050).
false_positives: Windows Hello for Business enrollment. Those are written by the computer account of the device, for the user who enrolled.

rules.title: Service principal name added to a user account (targeted Kerberoasting)
rules.description: Event 5136 writing servicePrincipalName on a user object. With write rights on a user, an attacker can add any SPN, request a service ticket for it and crack the user's password offline, then remove the SPN again.
triage: Check for an RC4 service ticket for that account right after (DL-0047) and whether the SPN was removed again.
Reset the account's password to a long random value.
false_positives: Admins creating a service account for a new application.

rules.title: Permissions changed on AdminSDHolder or the domain root
rules.description: Event 5136 changing nTSecurityDescriptor on CN=AdminSDHolder or on the domain object itself. An ACE on AdminSDHolder is copied to every protected group and admin account every hour. An ACE on the domain root can grant DCSync rights. Both are persistence that survives password resets.
triage: Compare the ACL with a known good copy and remove principals that should not be there.
On AdminSDHolder, wait for or force SDProp after the fix, then check protected accounts again.
false_positives: Rare. Some identity products need rights on the domain root at install time.

rules.title: Member added to a privileged domain group
rules.description: Events 4728, 4732 and 4756 (member added to a global, local or universal group) for Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, Schema Admins, Administrators and the operator groups. These groups change rarely, so every addition deserves a look.
triage: Confirm with the person who made the change (subject account). If nobody expected it, remove the member and reset the account.
Look at the member's recent logons and what they touched with the new rights.
false_positives: Planned admin changes. Match them against change tickets.

rules.title: SID history added to an account
rules.description: Events 4765 and 4766 are written when SID history is added to an account, or the attempt fails. A SID from a privileged group in SID history gives those rights everywhere the SID is accepted, including across trusts without SID filtering. Outside a domain migration this should never happen.
triage: Read the SID added. -519 (Enterprise Admins) or -512 (Domain Admins) from another domain means a trust attack.
Clear SID history on the account and make sure SID filtering is on for external and forest trusts.
false_positives: Domain migrations with ADMT. Those are planned and run from the migration account.

triage: Check the subject account and whether a change was planned. If not, reset the DSRM password and check DL-0041 on the same DC.
false_positives: DC builds and planned DSRM password rotation.

rules.title: Logon with new credentials (logon type 9, overpass-the-hash)
rules.description: Event 4624 with logon type 9 and the seclogo logon process. It is what runas /netonly creates, and also what mimikatz sekurlsa::pth and Rubeus createnetonly create when they start a process that uses a stolen hash or ticket for network access.
triage: Find the process that started the logon session and what it connected to.
Any type 9 logon on a workstation of a normal user is worth asking about.
false_positives: Admins using runas /netonly to manage other domains. Baseline the hosts and accounts.

rules.title: Certificate issued with a subject alternative name supplied in the request
rules.description: CA event 4886 or 4887 where the request attributes carry a SAN (san:upn=...). If the template lets the requester choose the subject (ESC1), or the CA accepts SAN attributes (ESC6), any user can get a certificate for an administrator and log on with it.
triage: Compare the requester with the identity in the SAN. A normal user asking for an admin's UPN is an attack.
Revoke the certificate and remove ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT or the EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 flag.
false_positives: Web server or device templates where the requester supplies DNS names by design. Exclude those templates.

rules.title: Remote access to the print spooler or EFS pipe (authentication coercion)
rules.description: Event 5145 for IPC$ with the spoolss or efsrpc pipe. Printer bug (MS-RPRN) and PetitPotam (MS-EFSR) and DFSCoerce (MS-DFSNM) force a server, often a DC, to authenticate to an attacker-chosen host. With unconstrained delegation on that host, the attacker captures the DC's TGT.
triage: Check the source IP. A workstation calling the spooler on a DC is suspicious.
Look for a TGT for the DC computer account appearing on another host (Rubeus monitor, DL-0031).
false_positives: Print servers receiving normal spooler traffic. Turn off the spooler on DCs and this becomes quiet there.
rules.xql:
config case_sensitive = false
| dataset = xdr_data
| filter event_type = ENUM.EVENT_LOG
| alter evt_subject_user = json_extract_scalar(action_evtlog_data_fields, "$.SubjectUserName"), evt_target_user = json_extract_scalar(action_evtlog_data_fields, "$.TargetUserName"), evt_share_name = json_extract_scalar(action_evtlog_data_fields, "$.ShareName"), evt_share_target = json_extract_scalar(action_evtlog_data_fields, "$.RelativeTargetName")
| filter action_evtlog_event_id = 5145 and evt_share_name ~= "(?i)IPC\\$$" and evt_share_target in ("spoolss", "efsrpc", "netdfs")

| limit 1000

`wineventlog`
| where EventCode=5145 AND match(ShareName, "(?i)IPC\\$$") AND (lower(RelativeTargetName)="spoolss" OR lower(RelativeTargetName)="efsrpc" OR lower(RelativeTargetName)="netdfs")
| table _time host EventCode SubjectUserName TargetUserName Message
| sort - _time

rules.title: Web server or PHP worker starts a shell or download tool (Linux)
rules.description: Apache, nginx, PHP-FPM, php-cgi, FrankenPHP or LiteSpeed starting sh, bash, curl, wget, netcat, Python or a recon command. This is the most direct sign that a remote code execution bug or a web shell is being used, for example PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), where the command runs as the web user (www-data) under the worker.
rules.condition_text: web_parent and shell_or_tool and not mail
triage: Read the full process tree under the worker. A reverse shell (DL-0064), a download into /tmp or /dev/shm, or id / uname right after a burst of PHP memory errors (DL-0066) points to exploitation.
Before you restart PHP, capture the worker's memory and the Apache logs. A restart erases the evidence.
Patch PHP (8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, 8.5.12 or your vendor backport) and restart every worker.
false_positives: PHP mail() runs sh -c sendmail (excluded). Applications that shell out to ImageMagick, git or a converter through sh -c. Baseline them per host.
rules.xql:
config case_sensitive = false
| dataset = xdr_data
| filter event_type = ENUM.PROCESS and event_sub_type = ENUM.PROCESS_START
| filter (actor_process_image_path ~= "(?i)/(apache2|httpd|nginx|php-fpm[0-9.]*|php-cgi[0-9.]*|frankenphp|lsphp[0-9]*|litespeed|lshttpd)$" and action_process_image_path ~= "(?i)/(sh|bash|dash|zsh|ksh|busybox|nc|ncat|netcat|socat|curl|wget|python[0-9.]*|perl|ruby|id|whoami|uname|hostname|base64|chmod)$") and not ((action_process_image_command_line != null and (action_process_image_command_line contains "sendmail" or action_process_image_command_line contains "/usr/sbin/exim" or action_process_image_command_line contains "postdrop")))
| fields _time, agent_hostname, actor_effective_username, actor_process_image_name, action_process_image_name, action_process_image_command_line
| sort desc _time
| limit 1000
rules.spl:
`sysmon` EventCode=1
| eval process_name=lower(mvindex(split(Image,"\\"),-1)), parent_name=lower(mvindex(split(ParentImage,"\\"),-1))
| where (match(ParentImage, "(?i)/(apache2|httpd|nginx|php-fpm[0-9.]*|php-cgi[0-9.]*|frankenphp|lsphp[0-9]*|litespeed|lshttpd)$") AND match(Image, "(?i)/(sh|bash|dash|zsh|ksh|busybox|nc|ncat|netcat|socat|curl|wget|python[0-9.]*|perl|ruby|id|whoami|uname|hostname|base64|chmod)$")) AND NOT ((isnotnull(CommandLine) AND (match(CommandLine, "(?i)sendmail") OR match(CommandLine, "(?i)/usr/sbin/exim") OR match(CommandLine, "(?i)postdrop"))))
| table _time host User ParentImage Image CommandLine
| sort - _time

rules.title: Reverse shell one-liner on Linux
rules.description: Command lines that connect a shell back to an attacker: bash with /dev/tcp, bash -i, netcat or ncat with -e or -c, mkfifo pipes, socat exec, or Python and Perl socket one-liners. After a web exploit this is usually the first thing run.
triage: Isolate the host. Take the remote IP and port from the command line and block them at the edge.
Find the parent. A web server or PHP worker parent means a web exploit (DL-0063); check the web logs around that time.
false_positives: Admin scripts that test a port with bash /dev/tcp. They do not start an interactive shell.
rules.xql:
config case_sensitive = false
| dataset = xdr_data
| filter event_type = ENUM.PROCESS and event_sub_type = ENUM.PROCESS_START
| filter action_process_image_command_line ~= "(?i)(/dev/(tcp|udp)/|\\bbash\\s+-i\\b|\\bnc(at)?\\b.*\\s-(e|c)\\s|mkfifo\\s|socat\\b.*exec:|socket\\.socket\\(|pty\\.spawn\\(|IO::Socket::INET)"
| fields _time, agent_hostname, actor_effective_username, actor_process_image_name, action_process_image_name, action_process_image_command_line
| sort desc _time
| limit 1000
rules.spl:
`sysmon` EventCode=1
| eval process_name=lower(mvindex(split(Image,"\\"),-1)), parent_name=lower(mvindex(split(ParentImage,"\\"),-1))
| where match(CommandLine, "(?i)(/dev/(tcp|udp)/|\\bbash\\s+-i\\b|\\bnc(at)?\\b.*\\s-(e|c)\\s|mkfifo\\s|socat\\b.*exec:|socket\\.socket\\(|pty\\.spawn\\(|IO::Socket::INET)")
| table _time host User ParentImage Image CommandLine
| sort - _time

rules.title: PHP file written in the web root by the web server or PHP worker
rules.description: The web server or PHP worker creating a .php, .phtml or .phar file under the web root. After remote code execution, attackers drop a web shell so they can come back even after the bug is patched.
triage: Open the file. Short files with eval, base64_decode, system, passthru or assert are web shells.
Find the first request that hit the new file in the access log; that source IP is the attacker.
false_positives: CMS core and plugin updates (WordPress, Drupal) written by the PHP worker. Correlate with an update in the admin panel.
rules.xql:
config case_sensitive = false
| dataset = xdr_data
| filter event_type = ENUM.FILE and event_sub_type in (ENUM.FILE_CREATE_NEW, ENUM.FILE_WRITE)
| filter actor_process_image_path ~= "(?i)/(apache2|httpd|nginx|php-fpm[0-9.]*|php-cgi[0-9.]*|frankenphp|lsphp[0-9]*|dash|sh|bash|curl|wget)$" and action_file_path ~= "(?i)^/(var/www|srv/www|srv/http|usr/share/nginx)/.+\\.(php[0-9]?|phtml|phar|pht)$"
| fields _time, agent_hostname, actor_process_image_name, action_file_path
| sort desc _time
| limit 1000
rules.spl:
`sysmon` EventCode=11
| eval process_name=lower(mvindex(split(Image,"\\"),-1)), file_name=lower(mvindex(split(TargetFilename,"\\"),-1))
| where match(Image, "(?i)/(apache2|httpd|nginx|php-fpm[0-9.]*|php-cgi[0-9.]*|frankenphp|lsphp[0-9]*|dash|sh|bash|curl|wget)$") AND match(TargetFilename, "(?i)^/(var/www|srv/www|srv/http|usr/share/nginx)/.+\\.(php[0-9]?|phtml|phar|pht)$")
| table _time host Image TargetFilename
| sort - _time

rules.title: PHP ran out of memory before any script line ran (PHP2Shell probe)
rules.description: "Allowed memory size ... exhausted" with "Unknown on line 0" means PHP hit memory_limit while parsing the request, before the application started. CVE-2026-109618 is triggered exactly this way, with a large multipart POST, so a few of these from one client can be a PHP2Shell attempt. A successful exploit can still return HTTP 200, so do not wait for a crash.
triage: Count these per client IP over a few minutes. Five or more from one source is a strong signal (see the correlation query on the rule page).
Check the same host for a shell under the web worker (DL-0063) and new PHP files in the web root (DL-0065).
Confirm the PHP version is patched and session.upload_progress.enabled is 0 until it is.
false_positives: Very large legitimate form posts on servers with a small memory_limit. They come from known users and repeat the same URL.
rules.xql:
config case_sensitive = false
| dataset = apache_httpd_raw
| filter _raw_log != null
| filter _raw_log contains "allowed memory size of" and _raw_log contains "exhausted" and _raw_log contains "unknown on line 0"
| fields _time, _raw_log
| sort desc _time
| limit 1000
rules.spl:
`apache_error`
| where match(_raw, "(?i)allowed\\ memory\\ size\\ of") AND match(_raw, "(?i)exhausted") AND match(_raw, "(?i)unknown\\ on\\ line\\ 0")
| table _time host _raw
| sort - _time

no_match.log.message: [Thu Oct 22 09:14:02.118262 2026] [php:error] [pid 46981] [client 198.51.100.23:51522] PHP Fatal error:  Allowed memory size of 134217728 bytes exhausted (tried to allocate 20480 bytes) in /var/www/html/report.php on line 88

rules.title: Web server or PHP-FPM worker crashed with a segmentation fault
rules.description: Apache AH00051 / AH00052 "exit signal Segmentation fault" or PHP-FPM "exited on signal 11 (SIGSEGV)". Memory corruption exploits such as PHP2Shell often crash a few workers before one attempt works, so crashes on an internet-facing PHP server are worth a look.
triage: Look at the requests just before the crash (access log, same second). Large multipart POSTs from one source point to exploitation.
Check for PHP memory errors from the same client (DL-0066) and for processes under the worker (DL-0063).
false_positives: Buggy PHP extensions or modules that crash under load. Those crash at the same code path every time; check with the vendor.
rules.xql:
config case_sensitive = false
| dataset = apache_httpd_raw
| filter _raw_log != null
| filter _raw_log ~= "(?i)ah0005[12].*segmentation fault" or _raw_log contains "exited on signal 11"
| fields _time, _raw_log
| sort desc _time
| limit 1000
rules.spl:
`apache_error`
| where match(_raw, "(?i)ah0005[12].*segmentation fault") OR match(_raw, "(?i)exited\\ on\\ signal\\ 11")
| table _time host _raw
| sort - _time

[22-Oct-2026 09:14:03] WARNING: [pool www] child 2231 exited on signal 11 (SIGSEGV) after 41.2 seconds from start

rules.title: FortiGate admin login through FortiCloud SSO or from an internet address
rules.description: A successful administrator login on a FortiGate that used FortiCloud SSO, or that came from an address outside RFC 1918. The 2026 FortiGate campaigns (CVE-2025-59718, CVE-2025-59719, CVE-2026-24858) all start this way: a crafted SAML login or an attacker's own FortiCloud account gives admin access in seconds, from the internet. Needs only the FortiGate event log, so it works for clients that send nothing else.
rules.condition_text: admin_login_ok and (sso or sso_ui or not internal_source)
triage: Check the source IP against the IOCs in the Fortinet advisories (FG-IR-26-060) and look at what the session did next. Config download (DL-0070), new admin (DL-0069) or a permissive policy (DL-0071) within minutes means compromise.
Confirm the firmware is patched and set admin-forticloud-sso-login to disable under config system global until it is.
Restrict the management interface to trusted hosts. An admin GUI reachable from the internet is the root problem.
false_positives: Admins who really use FortiCloud SSO. List them and confirm each login with the person.
Management from a provider or MSSP public IP. Allow-list those exact addresses, never a whole range.
rules.xql:

rules.title: New administrator account created on a FortiGate
rules.description: An object was added under system.admin. Attackers who get into a FortiGate create their own admin, often with a generic name (support, ssl-admin, backup, itadmin, secadmin, svcadmin), so they keep access after the bug is patched. Admin accounts are created a few times a year, so every hit deserves a look. FortiGate event log only.
triage: Read who created it (user), from where (ui shows the method and IP) and when. A creator that logged in through SSO or from the internet (DL-0068) is a compromise until proven otherwise.

Some implants delete their admin after use, so look for an Add and a Delete of the same cfgobj close together.
false_positives: A planned change by your own team. Match it to a change ticket and to the admin who made it (user and ui fields).

rules.title: FortiGate configuration backed up or downloaded
rules.description: The full FortiGate configuration was exported. It holds the LDAP bind account, VPN and admin secrets protected with reversible encryption, plus the network map. In the 2026 campaigns, stealing it was the first thing attackers did, then they decrypted the LDAP service account and walked into Active Directory. FortiGate event log only. Message wording differs a little between FortiOS versions, so the rule matches on the description and the message text.
triage: Treat an export by an unexpected user, from an internet IP or right after a new admin (DL-0069) as a credential theft. Rotate every secret in the file - the LDAP or AD bind account first, then VPN pre-shared keys and local user passwords.
In AD, review logons by the FortiGate bind account from anywhere other than the FortiGate itself.
Exports from the CLI (show full-configuration in the GUI console) do not always log a backup event. Also look for ui=jsconsole sessions from unusual IPs.
false_positives: Scheduled backups by FortiManager or a backup script. They come from one known IP at a fixed time.
An admin taking a backup before an upgrade. Match it to the change ticket.

rules.description: A firewall policy was added or edited so that both the source and destination address are "all" and the action is accept. In one 2026 FortiGate intrusion the attacker added four such policies to open every zone to every other zone. Real admins rarely write an all-to-all accept rule, so it is a cheap, strong signal. FortiGate event log only.

false_positives: Temporary troubleshooting rules. They should have a ticket and be deleted the same day.

rules.description: A change under log.* that disables a syslog or FortiAnalyzer target, changes its server, or stops traffic logging. The PEERSTITCH implant (CVE-2025-61624, October 2026) stopped syslog and cleared crash logs to blind the SOC. This is often the last FortiGate event you receive, so pair it with a "device went silent" hunt. FortiGate event log only.

false_positives: Planned SIEM or collector migrations. They change the server address once, with a ticket.

rules.description: A new automation stitch, trigger, action or auto-script. These run CLI commands on a schedule or on an event, which makes them a quiet place to hide persistence. false_positives: Your own stitches (email on admin login, config backup to FortiManager). They change rarely and through a known admin.

rules.title: MeshAgent or Pulseway started, or a program run from ProgramData\USOShared
rules.description: Remote management agents that the IT team did not deploy, or any executable started from C:\ProgramData\USOShared, a Windows Update folder that normally holds logs, not programs. In a 2026 FortiGate intrusion the attackers moved from the firewall to the servers, installed Pulseway and MeshAgent there, and hid MeshAgent from the uninstall list. Full-telemetry tier: needs an EDR on the servers behind the FortiGate.
triage: Find how the agent arrived (parent process, the logon that started it) and which server it calls home to.
Check the uninstall keys for SystemComponent=1 on the same host. A hidden RMM agent is a backdoor.
Walk back to the firewall. Look for a FortiGate admin login, config export or new admin in the days before (DL-0068 to DL-0070).
false_positives: An MSP or IT team that really uses MeshCentral or Pulseway. Allow-list the signer and the install path they use.
